superposition: The principle that magnetic fields from multiple sources add as vectors at every point, so complex patterns arise from simple current arrangements.
symmetry of maxwell's equations: The balanced relation in which a changing B field creates an E field via Faraday's law and a changing E field creates a B field via the Ampère-Maxwell law.
systematic procedure: A step-by-step problem-solving approach that requires identifying all relevant vectors and applying rules physically before drawing conclusions.
tangent: At any point around a wire, the magnetic field direction is tangent to the circular field line through that point and perpendicular to the radius.
terminal velocity in induction: The constant velocity reached when the electromagnetic drag force on induced currents exactly balances the applied force, marking steady-state operation.
time constant, τ: In an LR circuit, τ = L/R, the time for current to reach about 63% of its final value when building up or decay to about 37% when falling.
torque on a current loop: The rotational effect on a current loop in a field as opposite sides feel equal and opposite forces forming a couple, τ = NIAB sinφ.
transient response: The brief period when DC is first applied to a transformer, while current builds and flux changes, producing a temporary induced emf that vanishes at steady state.
transmission voltage: The voltage at which power is sent over long distances, often hundreds of thousands of volts, chosen to minimize resistive losses in the lines.
transverse wave: A wave whose oscillating quantity is perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation, contrasted with longitudinal waves.
turn density: The number of wire turns per unit length of a solenoid, which sets the magnetic field strength inside it, B = μ₀nI.
two-stage particle analysis: A method that treats a charged particle's motion in two steps, such as a velocity selector followed by magnetic deflection in a mass spectrometer.
two-step mechanism: A description of electromagnetic induction as a changing magnetic flux creating an electric field that then drives charge, separating cause from effect.
unification of optics and electromagneti: Maxwell's insight that light is an electromagnetic wave, merging the study of optics with electricity and magnetism.
uniform field: A field that is constant in magnitude and direction throughout a region, represented by evenly spaced parallel field lines.
van allen radiation belts: Zones of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field, spiraling along field lines between the magnetic poles.
vector diagram: A drawing that represents physical quantities as arrows, used to find the direction of magnetic forces, fields, and velocities.
velocity selector: A device with perpendicular electric and magnetic fields that passes only particles whose speed makes the two forces cancel, v = E/B.
voltage spike: A sudden large induced emf produced when current through an inductor is interrupted abruptly, since the flux changes rapidly.
wave equation: The differential equation governing wave propagation, whose electromagnetic form predicts waves traveling at the speed of light.
wavelength, λ: The spatial distance over which a wave repeats, related to frequency and speed by v = fλ.
weber: The SI unit of magnetic flux, equal to one tesla times one square meter, or one volt-second.
afocal system: An optical system with no net focal point, producing parallel output rays from parallel input rays, as in a telescope adjusted for relaxed viewing.
airy disk: The central bright spot of the circular diffraction pattern from a lens or aperture, surrounded by faint rings, that limits resolution.
analyzer: A second polarizer used to measure or control the polarization of light, transmitting an intensity that depends on its angle to the first.
angle of incidence: The angle between an incoming ray and the normal to a surface at the point of contact.
angle of reflection: The angle between a reflected ray and the normal, equal to the angle of incidence by the law of reflection.
angular magnification: The ratio of the angular size of an image to that of the object seen by the unaided eye, used for telescopes and microscopes.
angular resolution: The smallest angular separation at which two point sources can be distinguished, set by the diffraction limit of an optical system.
angular width: The angular spread of a diffraction feature such as the central maximum, increasing as the aperture or slit narrows.
anti reflection coating: A thin film on a lens that uses destructive interference of reflected light to reduce glare and increase transmission.
aperture diameter: The width of an optical opening, which sets the amount of light gathered and the diffraction-limited resolution.
bessel function: A mathematical function describing the intensity distribution of the circular diffraction pattern through an aperture, setting the Airy disk size.
black film: A soap film so thin that reflected light interferes destructively across all visible wavelengths, appearing dark.
boundary conditions: The physical requirements electromagnetic fields must satisfy at an interface, governing reflection, refraction, and phase shifts.
brewster's angle: The angle of incidence at which reflected light is completely polarized, where the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.
center of curvature: The center of the sphere of which a curved mirror or lens surface is a part, lying on the principal axis.
central maximum: The bright central region of a diffraction or interference pattern, the widest and most intense fringe.
chiral molecule: A molecule lacking mirror symmetry, which rotates the plane of polarized light passing through its solution.
coherence: The property of waves maintaining a constant phase relationship, required to produce stable interference patterns.
coherent light: Light whose waves keep a fixed phase relationship, such as laser light, enabling clear interference.
concave lens: A diverging lens, thinner at the center, that spreads parallel rays apart and forms reduced virtual images.
concave mirror: A mirror curved inward that converges parallel rays to a focal point and can form real or virtual images.
constructive interference: The reinforcement of waves that meet in phase, producing a combined amplitude larger than either alone.
converging lens: A convex lens, thicker at the center, that brings parallel rays to a focal point and can form real images.
convex mirror: A mirror curved outward that diverges parallel rays and always forms reduced, upright virtual images.
critical angle: The angle of incidence beyond which total internal reflection occurs at a boundary to a less dense medium.
crossed polarizers: Two polarizers with perpendicular transmission axes, which together block essentially all light.
destructive interference: The cancellation of waves that meet out of phase, producing a combined amplitude smaller than either alone.
diffraction minimum: A point of zero intensity in a diffraction pattern, occurring where waves from across the aperture cancel.
diffraction spreading: The bending and broadening of waves as they pass through an opening, increasing as the opening narrows toward the wavelength.
diverging lens: A lens that spreads parallel rays apart as if from a virtual focal point, forming reduced upright virtual images.
electric field projection: The component of a light wave's electric field along a polarizer's transmission axis, which determines the transmitted amplitude.
fiber optics: The guiding of light along thin glass fibers by total internal reflection, used for communication and imaging.
first order maximum: The first bright fringe on either side of the central maximum in an interference pattern, where the path difference equals one wavelength.
focal length: The distance from a lens or mirror to its focal point, where parallel rays converge or appear to diverge from.
focal length ratio: The ratio of the objective to eyepiece focal lengths, which sets a telescope's angular magnification.
focal point: The point at which a lens or mirror brings parallel rays to a focus, or from which they appear to diverge.
fringe spacing: The distance between adjacent bright or dark bands in an interference pattern, proportional to wavelength and screen distance.
geometric optics limit: The regime where wavelength is negligible compared to objects, so light is treated as straight rays and diffraction is ignored.
huygens principle: The principle that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets whose envelope forms the next wavefront.
image distance: The distance from a lens or mirror to the image it forms, positive for real images and negative for virtual ones.
in phase: The condition of two waves whose crests and troughs align, leading to constructive interference.
incoherent light: Light whose waves have random, shifting phase relationships, such as from a bulb, which cannot produce stable interference.
index of refraction: The ratio of light's speed in vacuum to its speed in a material, quantifying how much the medium slows and bends light.
intermediate image: The real image formed by the objective of a microscope or telescope, which the eyepiece then magnifies.
inverted image: An image oriented upside down relative to the object, characteristic of real images from converging optics.
iridescence: Color that shifts with viewing angle, produced by thin-film interference, as in soap bubbles and some animal surfaces.
lateral displacement: The sideways shift of a light ray after passing through a parallel-sided slab, due to refraction at both surfaces.
law of reflection: The law that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, both measured from the normal.
linear magnification: The ratio of image height to object height, indicating how much larger or smaller the image is and whether it is inverted.
linearly polarized light: Light whose electric field oscillates in a single fixed plane.
magnification: The factor by which an optical system enlarges or reduces an object, given by image height over object height.
minimum resolvable angle: The smallest angle between two sources that an optical system can distinguish, set by the Rayleigh criterion.
minimum thickness: The smallest film thickness producing a given interference condition for a particular wavelength.
normal: The line perpendicular to a surface at the point of incidence, from which angles of incidence and refraction are measured.
normal adjustment: A telescope setting in which the final image is at infinity, letting the relaxed eye view distant objects.
normal incidence: Light striking a surface along the normal, with an angle of incidence of zero.
normal line: The reference line perpendicular to a surface used to measure the angles of incident, reflected, and refracted rays.
numerical aperture: A measure of a lens's light-gathering ability and resolving power, equal to the refractive index times the sine of the half-angle of acceptance.
object distance: The distance from an object to a lens or mirror, used with the thin-lens or mirror equation to find the image.
objective lens: The lens nearest the object in a telescope or microscope, which forms the first real image.
optical activity: The ability of a chiral substance to rotate the plane of polarized light passing through it.
optical center: The central point of a lens through which a ray passes without changing direction.
optical path length: The product of physical distance and refractive index, representing the equivalent distance in vacuum for phase calculations.
optically denser medium: A medium with a higher refractive index, in which light travels more slowly and toward which it bends when entering.
order number m: The integer labeling each bright or dark fringe in an interference or diffraction pattern by its number of wavelengths of path difference.
order of interference: The integer indicating how many whole wavelengths of path difference correspond to a given interference fringe.
p-polarization: Light whose electric field oscillates in the plane of incidence, the component fully transmitted at Brewster's angle.
path difference: The difference in distance traveled by two interfering waves, which determines whether they combine constructively or destructively.
path length difference: The extra distance one of two interfering waves travels, setting the interference condition in terms of wavelengths.
phase shift on reflection: The half-wavelength phase change of light reflecting off a medium of higher refractive index, important in thin-film interference.
plane of incidence: The plane containing the incident ray and the surface normal, used to define polarization directions.
polarimetry: The measurement of the rotation of polarized light by an optically active substance to find its concentration.
polarizer: A device that transmits light of one polarization direction while blocking the perpendicular component.
principal axis: The central line through a lens or mirror, perpendicular to its surface and passing through its focal points.
principal ray: A standard ray with predictable behavior used to locate an image in a ray diagram.
principal rays: The set of standard rays used in ray diagrams to locate an image formed by a lens or mirror.
prism: A transparent block that refracts and disperses light, separating it into its component colors.
radius of curvature: The radius of the sphere of which a curved mirror or lens surface forms a part, twice the focal length for a mirror.
ray extension: The backward continuation of diverging rays to locate a virtual image behind a lens or mirror.
rayleigh criterion: The condition that two sources are just resolvable when the central maximum of one diffraction pattern falls on the first minimum of the other.
rayleigh scattering: The scattering of light by particles much smaller than its wavelength, stronger for shorter wavelengths, which makes the sky blue.
real image: An image formed where light rays actually converge, which can be projected onto a screen and is inverted.
refracting telescope: A telescope using lenses, with an objective forming a real image that an eyepiece magnifies.
refraction: The bending of light as it passes between media of different refractive indices due to a change in speed.
refractive index: The ratio of light's speed in vacuum to its speed in a medium, measuring how much the medium slows and bends light.
s-polarization: Light whose electric field oscillates perpendicular to the plane of incidence, the component strongly reflected at Brewster's angle.
screen distance l: The distance from a slit or aperture to the observation screen in an interference setup, which scales the fringe spacing.
small angle approximation: The simplification that sinθ ≈ tanθ ≈ θ for small angles, used to relate fringe positions to angles in interference.
spatial coherence: The correlation of phase across the width of a wavefront, required for clear interference between separated points.
specific rotation: A characteristic constant giving the angle an optically active substance rotates polarized light per unit concentration and path length.
spectral order: The integer m labeling each diffracted beam from a grating by the number of wavelengths of path difference.
temporal coherence: The correlation of a wave's phase over time, related to how monochromatic the light is and how long interference persists.
thin lens equation: The relation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i connecting focal length, object distance, and image distance for a thin lens.
total internal reflection: The complete reflection of light at a boundary to a less dense medium when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
transmission axis: The direction along which a polarizer passes the electric field component of light.
tube length: The separation between the objective and eyepiece of a microscope, which affects its magnification.
upright image: An image oriented the same way as the object, characteristic of virtual images.
virtual focal point: The point from which diverging rays appear to originate after passing through a diverging lens or convex mirror.
virtual image: An image from which rays only appear to diverge, which cannot be projected on a screen and is upright.
wavelength in medium: The wavelength of light within a material, shortened from its vacuum value by the refractive index.
working distance: The space between a microscope objective and the specimen when the image is in focus.
absorption: The taking up of photon energy by an atom or material, raising electrons to higher energy levels or producing heat.
absorption spectrum: The pattern of dark lines in a continuous spectrum where specific wavelengths have been absorbed by a substance's atoms.
accelerator mass spectrometry, ams: A highly sensitive technique that counts individual rare isotope atoms by accelerating and magnetically separating them, used in radiocarbon dating.
activity: The rate at which a radioactive sample decays, equal to the decay constant times the number of nuclei, measured in becquerels.
alpha decay: A radioactive decay in which a nucleus emits an alpha particle, reducing its mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2.
alpha particle: A helium-4 nucleus of two protons and two neutrons emitted in alpha decay.
atomic mass unit: A unit of mass equal to one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom, used to express atomic and nuclear masses.
atomic number z: The number of protons in a nucleus, which identifies the element.
balmer series: The set of hydrogen spectral lines from electron transitions to the n = 2 level, several of which lie in visible light.
band of stability: The region on a chart of nuclides where the neutron-to-proton ratio gives stable nuclei.
beta minus decay: A decay in which a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, raising the atomic number by one.
beta plus decay: A decay in which a proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino, lowering the atomic number by one.
beta-minus decay: A decay in which a neutron becomes a proton with emission of an electron and an antineutrino, increasing atomic number by one.
beta-plus decay: A decay in which a proton becomes a neutron with emission of a positron and a neutrino, decreasing atomic number by one.
binding energy: The energy that holds a nucleus together, equal to the energy needed to separate it into its individual nucleons.
binding energy per nucleon: The nuclear binding energy divided by the number of nucleons, peaking near iron and indicating nuclear stability.
branching decay: Radioactive decay in which a nuclide can decay by more than one mode, each with its own probability.
calibration curve: A reference graph relating a measured quantity to a known value, used to correct radiometric dating results.
cascade transition: A series of successive electron transitions through intermediate levels, each emitting a photon as an atom returns to the ground state.
chain reaction: A self-sustaining sequence of nuclear fissions in which released neutrons trigger further fissions.
classical wave theory: The pre-quantum view of light as a continuous wave, which failed to explain the photoelectric effect.
compound nucleus: A short-lived excited nucleus formed when a target nucleus absorbs an incoming particle before decaying.
concordia diagram: A graph used in uranium-lead dating that plots two isotopic ratios to test whether a sample's ages agree.
continuous beta spectrum: The range of kinetic energies of emitted beta particles, explained by the energy shared with an accompanying neutrino.
cosmogenic production: The creation of isotopes such as carbon-14 by cosmic-ray interactions in the upper atmosphere.
coulomb barrier: The electrostatic repulsion two positively charged nuclei must overcome to fuse.
critical mass: The minimum mass of fissile material needed to sustain a nuclear chain reaction.
crystal lattice: The regular repeating arrangement of atoms in a solid, off which electron waves can diffract.
daughter nucleus: The nucleus produced when a parent nucleus undergoes radioactive decay.
davisson-germer experiment: The experiment that confirmed the wave nature of electrons by observing their diffraction from a crystal.
de broglie wavelength: The wavelength λ = h/p associated with a moving particle, expressing its wave nature.
decay constant, λ: The probability per unit time that a given nucleus decays, related to half-life by λ = ln2 / t₁/₂.
decay curve: A graph of the number of remaining radioactive nuclei versus time, showing exponential decline.
deuterium: The hydrogen isotope with one proton and one neutron, used as a fuel in nuclear fusion.
discordant age: A radiometric age that disagrees among methods or ratios, indicating loss or gain of isotopes since formation.
electron antineutrino: The nearly massless, chargeless particle emitted alongside the electron in beta-minus decay.
electron capture: A decay in which a nucleus absorbs an inner electron, converting a proton to a neutron and emitting a neutrino.
electron diffraction: The bending and interference of electron waves passing through or reflecting off a crystal, demonstrating their wave nature.
electron volt: A unit of energy equal to the energy gained by an electron accelerated through one volt, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
electrostatic repulsion: The repulsive Coulomb force between like charges, such as the protons that resist nuclear fusion.
emission: The release of a photon when an atom's electron drops to a lower energy level.
emission spectrum: The pattern of bright lines at specific wavelengths emitted as atoms drop between energy levels.
energy level diagram: A diagram showing the discrete allowed energies of an atom and the transitions between them.
excited state: An energy state of an atom above its ground state, occupied after absorbing energy.
femtometer: A unit of length equal to 10⁻¹⁵ m, the scale of atomic nuclei.
fissile material: A nuclide such as uranium-235 that can sustain a fission chain reaction with slow neutrons.
fourier synthesis: The construction of a localized wave packet by adding waves of many wavelengths, used to describe matter waves.
fractional mass defect: The mass defect expressed as a fraction of total mass, indicating the proportion of mass converted to binding energy.
frequency: The number of wave cycles per second, in hertz, which sets a photon's energy through E = hf.
gamma ray: A high-energy photon emitted when a nucleus drops from an excited to a lower energy state.
gamma spectroscopy: The analysis of gamma-ray energies emitted by a sample to identify its radioactive isotopes.
ground state: The lowest energy state of an atom, in which its electrons occupy the lowest available levels.
h-bar: The reduced Planck constant, h divided by 2π, used in quantum mechanics and the uncertainty principle.
half-life, t₁/₂: The time for half the nuclei in a radioactive sample to decay, constant for a given isotope.
heisenberg uncertainty principle: The principle that position and momentum cannot both be known precisely, with the product of their uncertainties at least h-bar/2.
interference pattern: The pattern of alternating bright and dark regions produced when coherent waves overlap, seen for light and matter waves.
internal conversion: A decay process in which an excited nucleus transfers energy directly to an inner electron, ejecting it instead of emitting a gamma ray.
ionization energy: The energy needed to remove an electron completely from an atom.
iron peak: The maximum in binding energy per nucleon near iron, marking the most stable nuclei and the boundary between fusion and fission energy release.
isobar: One of two or more nuclides with the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
isochron method: A radiometric dating technique that plots isotopic ratios across samples to find age without knowing initial amounts.
isotope: An atom of an element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
kinetic energy from potential: The kinetic energy a charged particle gains when accelerated through a potential difference, equal to qV.
lepton number: A conserved quantity assigned to leptons such as electrons and neutrinos, used to balance nuclear decay equations.
lyman series: The set of hydrogen spectral lines from electron transitions to the n = 1 level, lying in the ultraviolet.
mass defect: The difference between the mass of separated nucleons and the mass of the assembled nucleus, converted to binding energy.
mass number: The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.
mass number a: The total count of nucleons, protons plus neutrons, in a nucleus.
mass number conservation: The rule that the total number of nucleons is the same before and after a nuclear reaction.
mass-energy equivalence: Einstein's principle E = mc² that mass and energy are interconvertible, underlying nuclear binding energy.
matter waves: The wave behavior associated with moving particles, described by the de Broglie wavelength.
maximum kinetic energy: The greatest kinetic energy of photoelectrons, equal to the photon energy minus the work function.
momentum-energy relationship: The relation linking a particle's energy, momentum, and rest mass, E² = (pc)² + (mc²)².
neutron number n: The number of neutrons in a nucleus, equal to the mass number minus the atomic number.
nuclear fission: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons.
nuclear fusion: The joining of light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy, as in stars.
nucleon: A proton or neutron, one of the particles making up an atomic nucleus.
nucleon saturation: The leveling of binding energy per nucleon for large nuclei because each nucleon attracts only its nearest neighbors.
parent nucleus: The original nucleus that undergoes radioactive decay into a daughter nucleus.
parent nuclide: The original radioactive nuclide that decays into a daughter product, used in radiometric dating.
parent-to-daughter ratio: The ratio of remaining parent atoms to accumulated daughter atoms, used to determine a sample's age.
photocurrent: The electric current produced by photoelectrons ejected from a surface by incident light.
photoelectric equation: Einstein's relation that a photoelectron's maximum kinetic energy equals the photon energy minus the work function.
photon: A quantum of electromagnetic radiation carrying energy E = hf and behaving as a particle of light.
photon hypothesis: Einstein's proposal that light energy is delivered in discrete quanta, explaining the photoelectric effect.
photon wavelength: The wavelength of a photon, related to its energy by E = hc/λ.
planck constant h: The fundamental constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s relating a photon's energy to its frequency.
planck's constant: The fundamental constant relating photon energy to frequency, 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
potassium-argon dating: A radiometric method dating rocks by the decay of potassium-40 to argon-40.
principal quantum number n: The integer labeling an atom's energy levels, with higher values meaning greater energy and larger orbitals.
q-value: The energy released or absorbed in a nuclear reaction, equal to the mass difference times c².
quantization: The restriction of a physical quantity such as energy to discrete allowed values.
quantized energy levels: The discrete set of energies an electron may have in an atom, with transitions producing spectral lines.
quantum tunneling: The quantum effect allowing a particle to pass through an energy barrier it classically could not surmount, as in alpha decay.
radiogenic: Describing an isotope produced by radioactive decay, such as the argon accumulated from potassium decay.
spectral lines: The discrete bright or dark lines in an atomic spectrum produced by electron transitions between quantized energy levels.
stopping potential: The reverse voltage needed to stop the fastest photoelectrons, satisfying eV_stop = KE_max of the emitted electrons.
strong nuclear force: The fundamental force binding protons and neutrons in the nucleus, very strong at short range but vanishing beyond a few femtometers.
system closure: The moment a mineral stops exchanging parent and daughter isotopes with its surroundings, starting the radioactive clock used in dating.
three-body decay: A decay producing three particles, allowing the energy shared among products to vary continuously while conserving total energy and momentum.
threshold frequency: The minimum photon frequency able to eject electrons from a metal, given by f0 = work function divided by Planck's constant.
time delay: The classically predicted lag before electron emission, contradicted by the experimental finding that photoemission is essentially instantaneous.
transition energy: The energy difference between two atomic levels, equal to the photon energy emitted or absorbed when an electron moves between them.
tritium: A radioactive hydrogen isotope with one proton and two neutrons (mass number 3), having a half-life of about 12.3 years.
two-body decay: A decay producing exactly two particles, giving the products discrete kinetic energies fixed by conservation of energy and momentum.
uranium-lead dating: A radiometric method measuring U-238/Pb-206 and U-235/Pb-207 ratios in zircon, yielding two cross-checkable independent age estimates.
wave packet: A localized disturbance built by superposing waves of different wavelengths, representing a particle with defined position but uncertain momentum.
wave-particle duality: The principle that all matter and energy exhibit both wave-like and particle-like behavior depending on the experimental context.
weak nuclear force: The fundamental force responsible for beta decay, changing quark flavor inside nucleons through exchange of W and Z bosons.
work function: The minimum energy needed to free the most loosely bound electron from a metal surface, measured in electronvolts or joules.
